title: Solar sales rep
tagline: Learn to turn a knock on the door into a signed solar contract through trust and precise sizing.
setting: You walk suburban streets knocking on homeowner doors, standing on porches or driveways with a tablet and a shade-analysis app.

scenarios.label: Cold porch opening
scenarios.desc: Open a homeowner who is curious but guarded about solar.
scenarios.setup: You are a solar rep standing on the front porch. The homeowner opens the door and says: “Yeah? What’s this about?”
scenarios.objective: Earn permission to run a quick shade-and-bill analysis on the spot.
scenarios.moment: Tuesday 6:15 pm, golden light on the lawn

scenarios.label: Kitchen table sizing
scenarios.desc: Size the system to the homeowner’s real usage and explain buy-back rates.
scenarios.setup: You are at the kitchen table with a year of electric bills spread out. The homeowner says: “My neighbour got a tiny cheque from the utility. How do I know yours is different?”
scenarios.objective: Present a production guarantee and current net-metering rate that match their actual load.

scenarios.label: Incentive close
scenarios.desc: Close the deal when the homeowner hesitates on price despite the fit.
scenarios.setup: You have shown the design and savings. The homeowner leans back and says: “It still feels like a lot up front. What else you got?”
scenarios.objective: Secure a signed agreement using the expiring federal credit and the utility rebate that ends this month.
scenarios.moment: Same evening, 8:10 pm, streetlights clicking on

buyers.angle: Cares about carbon footprint more than savings.
Fixed income makes upfront cost scary.

buyers.role: homeowner with past solar scam experience
buyers.angle: Previous bad installer left deep distrust.

objections: My roof gets too much shade from the trees
I can’t afford the upfront cost even with financing
I don’t trust companies that call me out of the blue
My electric bill is too low to make it worth it
I need to check with my spouse first before deciding
The buy-back rate seems too low to save money
Installation will mess up my roof and cause leaks
I’ve heard solar doesn’t work well in our climate

rubric.label: Rapport building
rubric.what: Opens with genuine curiosity, listens before pitching, and mirrors the homeowner’s pace.

rubric.label: Usage qualifying
rubric.what: Asks for 12 months of bills, EV plans, and future loads before quoting a system size.

rubric.label: Rate transparency
rubric.what: States the current utility buy-back rate, cites the tariff sheet, and explains true-up periods.

rubric.label: Production guarantee
rubric.what: Presents a kWh guarantee with a clear shortfall remedy, not a vague promise.

rubric.label: Incentive accuracy
rubric.what: Quotes only live federal, state, and utility incentives with expiry dates and eligibility rules.

rubric.label: Compliance disclosure
rubric.what: Discloses licensing, lien position, cancellation rights, and data privacy before any signature.

pitfalls: Quoting last year’s net-metering rate instead of the current tariff.
Sizing the array to roof space instead of the homeowner’s actual kWh history.
Implying the tax credit is guaranteed without verifying tax appetite.
line: Selling rooftop solar door to door

research.text: Common objections to selling rooftop solar door to door include concerns about the system's fit for individual energy needs and the accuracy of buy-back rates. Sales reps should ask detailed questions to match the system size correctly and ensure they use current buy-back rates. Sales conversations often start with curiosity rather than pressure, addressing pain points like average electric bills, and establishing success stories from previous clients. The sales pitch builds trust through transparency and may introduce discounts, rebates, and incentives at the last minute. Despite the low conversion rate, door-to-door sales remain effective due to the personal connection and trust built through face-to-face conversations.

personas.name: Tom Whitaker
personas.background: Tom lives with his wife and two kids in a modest neighborhood. He works in construction and feels pressure to keep the household budget tight while watching his electric bills rise.
pushbacks: I can’t afford the upfront cost even with financing
My roof gets too much shade from the trees
I need to check with my spouse first before deciding

personas.name: Grace Thompson
personas.background: Grace teaches middle school science in her town and volunteers with the local climate action group. She installed solar panels on her own home two years ago and loves showing neighbors the data.
pushbacks: I already have solar panels on my house and they’ve cut my carbon emissions by forty percent
The upfront cost is a stretch even with financing but I’d rather invest in clean energy than keep paying coal companies
I’ve been researching this for months and I’m not impressed by door-to-door salespeople
wins_over: transparent pricing that honors community values
demonstrable impact on neighborhood carbon reduction

personas.name: Carl Hensley
personas.background: Carl retired from the town council after decades of service, and he values security over novelty. He watches his spending closely, especially when it comes to investments that affect his stable pension income. He and his partner enjoy modest comforts in a leafy neighborhood where winter heating bills still surprise the.
pushbacks: I can’t saddle my wife with a payment that’s not guaranteed
The numbers just don’t line up with what I’ve saved for years
My roof covers half the sky and the panels would waste my money

personas.name: Riley Chen
personas.background: Runs the home budget while caring for two kids. Sees energy costs climb each year and looks for steady ways to lower them.
pushbacks: The panels won’t help much when my trees are shading the roof
My husband and I need to review every expense together first
I can’t spend a big chunk of money right now, even with financing

personas.name: Lena Cho
personas.role: homeowner with past solar scam experience
personas.background: Lena moved to the suburbs after her husband retired. She was scammed by a solar company five years ago and now handles home repairs herself and watches every contract closely.
pushbacks: “I’ve already been burned once, I’m not signing anything else without proof.”
“My electric bill is low because I use very little power, so I’m not interested.”
“I need to talk to my daughter before I commit to anything.”
